subtopic_detail: Intensely itchy raised lesions arising within the abdominal stretch marks at 36 weeks with the navel spared
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 34 year old woman in her first pregnancy at 36 weeks gestation who has developed an intensely itchy rash over the past five days. She describes raised red patches that started in the silvery marks on her lower abdomen and have since spread to her thighs and buttocks.

The itch is worst in the evening and is disturbing her sleep. She has no itching of her palms or soles and no dark urine. She takes no regular medications and has no personal or family history of skin disease.

data_table.Examination: Erythematous urticated papules and plaques arising within the abdominal striae with coalescence into plaques on the outer thighs and buttocks, a clear rim of uninvolved skin immediately around the umbilicus, no vesicles or bullae anywhere, no excoriation of the palms or soles, symphysis fundal height appropriate for dates
data_table.Investigations: Liver function tests within normal limits, serum bile acids 4 micromol/L (less than 10), full blood count within normal limits, cardiotocograph normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence oral ursodeoxycholic acid and repeat the serum bile acids and liver function tests again in one week
options.rationale: Ursodeoxycholic acid treats intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy, in which the itch is worst on the palms and soles, there is no primary rash, and bile acids are elevated. Normal bile acids with a visible primary eruption rules that diagnosis out here. (Source: RANZCOG: Obstetric cholestasis)

options.text: Arrange induction of labour at 37 weeks gestation on the grounds that her symptoms are unlikely to settle before then
options.rationale: Early delivery is offered in pregnancy dermatoses only when there is a foetal risk, as with pemphigoid gestationis, and polymorphic eruption carries no such risk. Delivering a woman at 37 weeks for a benign itch exposes the baby to avoidable late preterm morbidity. (Source: RANZCOG: Skin conditions in pregnancy)

options.text: Arrange a skin biopsy with direct immunofluorescence and start systemic corticosteroids while awaiting the histology result
options.rationale: Immunofluorescence showing linear C3 along the basement membrane is how pemphigoid gestationis is confirmed, and that condition begins around the umbilicus and blisters, which is the exact inverse of this distribution. Biopsy is worth doing when bullae appear or when the periumbilical skin is the focus rather than the spared area. (Source: RANZCOG: Skin conditions in pregnancy)

options.text: Prescribe a potent topical corticosteroid ointment with emollients and explain that the rash resolves after the birth
options.rationale: Involvement of the striae with sparing of the periumbilical skin and an absence of blistering identifies polymorphic eruption of pregnancy, which is benign, carries no foetal risk and is controlled with topical corticosteroid and emollients until delivery. Symptoms settle within days to weeks after birth and recurrence in later pregnancies is uncommon. (Source: RANZCOG: Skin conditions in pregnancy)

options.text: Prescribe a topical antifungal cream for the abdominal and thigh lesions and review her again in the antenatal clinic in two weeks
options.rationale: Tinea and candidal intertrigo produce a scaly annular or satellite pattern in skin folds rather than urticated plaques arising within striae. An antifungal would be the correct choice for a well demarcated scaly ring with central clearing under the abdominal apron. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

explanation.summary: Polymorphic eruption of pregnancy, also known as pruritic urticarial papules and plaques of pregnancy, is the commonest specific dermatosis of pregnancy and typically appears in the third trimester of a first pregnancy, particularly where there has been rapid abdominal distension from a large baby or a multiple pregnancy. Its distribution is the diagnostic feature: lesions arise within the abdominal striae and characteristically spare a rim of skin around the umbilicus, then spread centrifugally to the thighs, buttocks and arms while sparing the face, palms and soles. The main differential is pemphigoid gestationis, an autoimmune blistering disease that begins periumbilically, forms tense bullae, and is associated with small for gestational age babies and preterm birth, so it needs biopsy and systemic treatment. Intrahepatic cholestasis is excluded by the presence of a primary rash and normal bile acids, since cholestatic itch is generalised without a primary eruption. Polymorphic eruption resolves spontaneously after delivery and is managed symptomatically.
key_points: Lesions within the striae with periumbilical sparing define polymorphic eruption of pregnancy.
Pemphigoid gestationis starts around the umbilicus, blisters, and carries foetal risk.
Normal bile acids with a visible primary rash exclude intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy.
Topical corticosteroid and emollients control symptoms until spontaneous resolution after birth.
No foetal surveillance or early delivery is required for polymorphic eruption.
explanation.pearls: Pemphigoid gestationis recurs in around three quarters of subsequent pregnancies and can flare with the combined oral contraceptive pill or at menstruation, so a woman with that diagnosis needs both prepregnancy counselling and a progestogen only or non hormonal contraceptive choice afterwards.

subtopic_detail: Disabling headache on the second postnatal day that is present on sitting up and gone within minutes of lying flat
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar asked to see a 29 year old woman on the postnatal ward two days after a normal vaginal birth with an epidural. She describes a severe headache across the front and back of her head that begins within a minute of sitting upright and disappears almost completely when she lies down.

She is unable to sit up to feed her baby and has not been out of bed today. The anaesthetic record documents a dural puncture with the epidural needle at insertion. She has no visual disturbance, no weakness and no convulsion.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Alert and orientated with no neck stiffness, no photophobia, no papilloedema on fundoscopy, cranial nerves intact with full eye movements, no focal limb weakness, reflexes symmetrical, no calf tenderness, epidural insertion site clean with no erythema or discharge
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, platelet count 244 x10^9/L (150 to 400), urine dipstick negative for protein, liver function tests within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue bed rest with regular paracetamol, oral caffeine and encouragement of oral fluids, and review her again in two days
options.rationale: Conservative therapy is a reasonable first response in the first day or for a mild headache, but the evidence that caffeine, fluids and bed rest alter the natural history is poor. Persisting with it in a woman who cannot sit up to feed her baby prolongs disability and delays bonding and mobilisation. (Source: Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists: Post dural puncture headache)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists: Post dural puncture headache

options.text: Arrange urgent computed tomography of the brain with venography to exclude cerebral venous sinus thrombosis as the cause
options.rationale: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis is the dangerous postnatal mimic, but its headache is progressive and non postural and is usually accompanied by focal signs, seizures or papilloedema, none of which are present. Imaging becomes mandatory if the headache loses its postural character or if any neurological sign appears. (Source: Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists: Post dural puncture headache)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists: Post dural puncture headache

options.text: Commence an intravenous magnesium sulfate infusion and start antihypertensive therapy for probable late onset pre-eclampsia
options.rationale: Postpartum pre-eclampsia does present with headache in the first week, but it comes with hypertension, proteinuria or deranged bloods, and her blood pressure, urine and liver tests are all normal. The strictly postural nature of this headache also does not fit a pre-eclamptic headache. (Source: RANZCOG: Hypertension in pregnancy)

options.text: Perform a diagnostic lumbar puncture to measure the opening pressure and analyse the cerebrospinal fluid for infection
options.rationale: Another dural puncture in a woman who already has a cerebrospinal fluid leak worsens the very problem being treated. Lumbar puncture is reserved for a genuine suspicion of meningitis, which would be signalled by fever, neck stiffness and a non postural headache. (Source: Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists: Post dural puncture headache)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists: Post dural puncture headache

options.text: Refer her to the anaesthetic team for an epidural blood patch after explaining the procedure and its likely benefits
options.rationale: A postural headache after a documented dural puncture that prevents a woman caring for her baby is a disabling post dural puncture headache, and an autologous epidural blood patch relieves symptoms in around three quarters of women, usually within an hour. Conservative measures alone leave her bed bound for days to weeks while the dural defect heals. (Source: Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists: Post dural puncture headache)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists: Post dural puncture headache

explanation.summary: Post dural puncture headache follows loss of cerebrospinal fluid through a dural defect, which lowers intracranial pressure and allows traction on pain sensitive intracranial structures when the woman sits or stands. The defining feature is its postural nature, appearing within minutes of sitting upright and relieved within minutes of lying flat, usually beginning between twelve and seventy two hours after the puncture. Associated features include neck stiffness, tinnitus, hearing change and photophobia, and a sixth nerve palsy is a recognised complication of prolonged traction. The critical clinical discipline is to keep reviewing the postural character, because a headache that becomes constant, or that is accompanied by any focal sign, seizure, fever or papilloedema, demands neuroimaging for cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, subdural haematoma or infection. Untreated, the headache usually settles within one to two weeks, but an epidural blood patch shortens that substantially and is offered when symptoms are severe or prolonged.
key_points: A headache that appears on sitting and resolves on lying flat is postural until proven otherwise.
Onset is typically twelve to seventy two hours after the dural puncture.
Loss of the postural character or any focal sign mandates urgent neuroimaging.
Epidural blood patch relieves symptoms in around three quarters of women.
Conservative measures have weak evidence and should not delay definitive treatment in disabling cases.
explanation.pearls: Women who have had a dural puncture during labour carry a raised risk of chronic headache and backache for years afterwards, so document the event clearly in the discharge summary and arrange anaesthetic follow up rather than leaving the woman to attribute ongoing symptoms to motherhood.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists: Post dural puncture headache
BMJ Best Practice: Post dural puncture headache

subtopic_detail: Constant localised pain over a known uterine fibroid at 26 weeks with a low grade temperature and a quiet cervix
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar seeing a 33 year old woman at 26 weeks gestation who presents with two days of constant pain in the right side of her abdomen. The pain does not come and go and she has felt hot and shivery at times.

A fibroid measuring 8 cm was documented on her 20 week ultrasound. She reports normal foetal movements, no vaginal bleeding and no fluid loss. She has passed urine without discomfort.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in room air, temperature 37.6 degrees Celsius, foetal heart rate 148 beats per minute
data_table.Examination: Tenderness localised over a firm mass palpable in the right side of the uterus, uterus otherwise soft and non tender with no palpable contractions, no offensive vaginal discharge, cervix long and closed on speculum examination
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 13.4 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), C-reactive protein 28 mg/L (less than 5), midstream urine microscopy showing no organisms and no white cells, ultrasound showing an 8 cm intramural fibroid with cystic change and reduced internal vascularity, normal liquor volume, cervical length 38 mm, cardiotocograph normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer her for myomectomy to remove the fibroid before the pain and inflammatory response worsen further during the pregnancy
options.rationale: Myomectomy during pregnancy carries a high risk of catastrophic haemorrhage and pregnancy loss because the fibroid vasculature is greatly expanded, so it is almost never performed. It is considered only for a pedunculated torted fibroid that cannot be managed conservatively. (Source: RANZCOG: Fibroids in pregnancy)

options.text: Give antenatal corticosteroids and commence nifedipine tocolysis on the basis that this pain represents established preterm labour
options.rationale: Preterm labour causes intermittent tightenings with cervical change, whereas this pain is constant and the cervix is long and closed with a reassuring cervical length. Tocolysis and steroids would be indicated if contractions with cervical shortening developed. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm labour)

options.text: Start intravenous ampicillin with gentamicin and metronidazole for presumed chorioamnionitis and plan delivery if the fever persists
options.rationale: Chorioamnionitis produces uterine tenderness that is generalised rather than confined to a mass, with offensive discharge, maternal and foetal tachycardia and usually ruptured membranes, none of which are present. The localisation of the tenderness to the fibroid itself is what separates the two. (Source: RANZCOG: Fibroids in pregnancy)

options.text: Admit her for analgesia with paracetamol and a short opioid course plus hydration, with observation and expected resolution over days
options.rationale: Localised tenderness over a fibroid with a low grade fever, mild leucocytosis and ultrasound cystic change and reduced vascularity is red degeneration, which is an ischaemic infarction of the fibroid as it outgrows its blood supply and settles conservatively over several days to two weeks. Analgesia and hydration are the whole of the treatment. (Source: RANZCOG: Fibroids in pregnancy)

options.text: Arrange diagnostic laparoscopy on the basis that appendicitis cannot be excluded in a pregnant woman with right sided abdominal pain
options.rationale: Appendicitis is the key surgical differential for right sided pain in pregnancy, but it migrates upward with gestation, causes anorexia and guarding, and would not show cystic change within a fibroid on ultrasound. Surgery is justified when imaging and examination point to the appendix rather than to a known fibroid. (Source: RANZCOG: Fibroids in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Fibroids enlarge under the hormonal and haemodynamic influences of pregnancy, and a proportion outgrow their blood supply and undergo red or carneous degeneration, most often in the second trimester and most often in fibroids larger than about 5 cm. The clinical picture is constant, well localised pain with tenderness confined to the fibroid, a low grade fever, mild leucocytosis and a modest rise in inflammatory markers, which together mimic infection convincingly enough that women are frequently given unnecessary antibiotics. Ultrasound supports the diagnosis when it shows cystic or heterogeneous change with reduced vascularity within the lesion. The condition is self limiting and resolves over several days to two weeks with analgesia and hydration, though the pain is often severe enough to require short term opioids. Non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs are effective but are used cautiously and briefly before 32 weeks because of effects on the ductus arteriosus and amniotic fluid.
key_points: Red degeneration causes constant pain localised over the fibroid rather than generalised uterine tenderness.
Low grade fever, leucocytosis and a raised C-reactive protein are expected and do not indicate infection.
Ultrasound showing cystic change with reduced vascularity within the fibroid supports the diagnosis.
Treatment is analgesia and hydration, with resolution over several days to two weeks.
Myomectomy in pregnancy risks catastrophic haemorrhage and is almost never indicated.
explanation.pearls: If a non steroidal anti inflammatory drug is used for red degeneration, keep the course under 48 hours and stop it by 32 weeks gestation, because prolonged exposure closes the ductus arteriosus prematurely and reduces foetal urine output enough to cause oligohydramnios.

subtopic_detail: Daily non prescribed oxycodone use disclosed at booking by a woman at 14 weeks who wants to stop straight away
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in an antenatal clinic booking a 26 year old woman at 14 weeks gestation in her second pregnancy. She discloses that she has been taking around 100 mg of non prescribed oxycodone daily for the past two years and that she injects nothing.

She tells you she is determined to be completely off everything before the baby arrives and asks you to help her stop this week. She has no medical comorbidities, her booking bloods including hepatitis and human immunodeficiency virus serology are pending, and her first child lives with her and her partner.

data_table.Examination: No stigmata of intravenous drug use, no needle marks, chest clear, abdomen soft with a uterus palpable just above the symphysis pubis, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound confirming a single live intrauterine pregnancy consistent with 14 weeks gestation, full blood count within normal limits, ferritin 42 micrograms/L (30 to 200)

lead_in: What would you first recommend to her?

options.text: Make an immediate child protection notification about the unborn baby and the older child before discussing treatment options with her
options.rationale: Leading with a statutory notification at disclosure is the single most reliable way to drive a pregnant woman out of antenatal care, and substance use alone without evidence of harm is not a threshold for notification in most Australian jurisdictions. Prenatal reporting is discussed openly with the woman and made when there are genuine concerns about the safety of a child. (Source: National Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Drug Use During Pregnancy, Birth and the Early Development Years)
source_refs: National Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Drug Use During Pregnancy, Birth and the Early Development Years

options.text: Admit her for a supervised rapid inpatient detoxification over the coming week while the pregnancy is still in the second trimester
options.rationale: Withdrawal in pregnancy raises catecholamine levels and has been associated with foetal distress and miscarriage or preterm birth, and relapse rates after detoxification alone exceed three quarters. Detoxification is considered only where the woman declines maintenance and can be supported intensively with close foetal monitoring. (Source: National Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Drug Use During Pregnancy, Birth and the Early Development Years)
source_refs: National Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Drug Use During Pregnancy, Birth and the Early Development Years

options.text: Commence oral naltrexone once she has stopped opioids for several days in order to block any further effect from opioid use
options.rationale: Naltrexone requires the woman to be fully withdrawn before it can be started, which imposes precisely the withdrawal that should be avoided, and safety data in pregnancy remain limited. It is an option for a woman already stable and abstinent who chooses it outside pregnancy. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Support her plan to cease abruptly this week with symptomatic medication only and review her in the antenatal clinic in two weeks
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation causes the most severe withdrawal of all the options and carries the highest relapse rate, often to a dose she is no longer tolerant to. Symptomatic treatment alone is appropriate only for a woman with a very low level of dependence who has declined all other options. (Source: National Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Drug Use During Pregnancy, Birth and the Early Development Years)
source_refs: National Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Drug Use During Pregnancy, Birth and the Early Development Years

options.text: Refer her urgently to a specialist drug and alcohol service for stabilisation on opioid agonist treatment alongside her antenatal care
options.rationale: Opioid agonist treatment with methadone or buprenorphine is the standard of care in pregnancy because it removes the cycles of intoxication and withdrawal that cause foetal distress, improves antenatal attendance and markedly improves birth outcomes. Australian guidance is explicit that maintenance, not abstinence, is the goal during pregnancy. (Source: National Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Drug Use During Pregnancy, Birth and the Early Development Years)
source_refs: National Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Drug Use During Pregnancy, Birth and the Early Development Years

explanation.summary: Opioid dependence in pregnancy is managed with agonist maintenance rather than withdrawal, because the stability it provides protects the foetus from the repeated episodes of withdrawal that accompany illicit use and because it anchors the woman in antenatal care. Both methadone and buprenorphine are acceptable in Australian practice, with buprenorphine associated with a shorter and milder neonatal abstinence syndrome and methadone associated with better retention in treatment for some women. Doses often need to increase through the third trimester as plasma volume and hepatic metabolism rise, and a woman whose dose is held static may report returning withdrawal symptoms late in pregnancy. Breastfeeding is encouraged on either agonist, as the amount transferred in milk is small and helps settle the neonate. Every such pregnancy needs planning for neonatal abstinence syndrome, which affects a majority of exposed babies and typically appears within the first three days for heroin, later for methadone, and requires a minimum observation period in hospital.
key_points: Opioid agonist maintenance, not detoxification, is the standard of care in pregnancy.
Withdrawal in pregnancy is associated with foetal distress and very high relapse rates.
Agonist doses frequently need to rise in the third trimester because of physiological changes.
Breastfeeding is encouraged on both methadone and buprenorphine.
Substance use alone is not a threshold for child protection notification in most jurisdictions.
explanation.pearls: Plan for a minimum of three to five days of neonatal observation after birth, and longer for methadone exposure, because neonatal abstinence syndrome from methadone can first appear beyond 72 hours of age and up to a week after the last maternal dose.

sources.label: National Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Drug Use During Pregnancy, Birth and the Early Development Years
BMJ Best Practice: Opioid use disorder

subtopic_detail: Third episode of severe right upper abdominal pain after fatty food at 18 weeks with gallstones and normal liver tests
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 30 year old woman at 18 weeks gestation who has just recovered from her third episode of severe pain under the right ribs. Each episode has come on an hour or two after a fatty meal, built over about half an hour, lasted around four hours and then faded completely.

She vomited during the current episode and is now comfortable and hungry. She has not been jaundiced and her urine and stool colour have been normal throughout.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft with no tenderness on deep palpation of the right upper quadrant between episodes, Murphy sign negative, no jaundice of the sclerae, uterus palpable at the level of the umbilicus
data_table.Investigations: Liver function tests within normal limits with a bilirubin of 12 micromol/L (less than 20), lipase 32 U/L (less than 60), white cell count 9.8 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), C-reactive protein less than 5 mg/L (less than 5), ultrasound showing multiple mobile gallstones with a normal gallbladder wall thickness and a common bile duct of 4 mm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Manage her conservatively with a low fat diet and analgesia, deferring any operation until at least six weeks after the birth
options.rationale: Expectant management in pregnancy is associated with recurrent attacks in more than half of women and a substantial rate of progression to cholecystitis, pancreatitis or admission, each of which carries its own foetal risk. It is a reasonable choice only for a single mild episode very late in the third trimester. (Source: RANZCOG: Non obstetric surgery in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Non obstetric surgery in pregnancy

options.text: Refer her for endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography with sphincterotomy to clear the biliary tree of the stones causing her pain
options.rationale: Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography treats stones in the common bile duct, and her bilirubin, liver enzymes and duct calibre are all normal, so there is nothing in the duct to clear. It would be indicated for obstructive jaundice or gallstone pancreatitis with a dilated duct. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Gallstone disease)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Gallstone disease

options.text: Refer her for laparoscopic cholecystectomy during this second trimester after discussing the risks of surgery and of continued symptoms
options.rationale: Recurrent symptomatic gallstones in pregnancy are best treated by laparoscopic cholecystectomy, and the second trimester is the optimal window because organogenesis is complete and the uterus is not yet large enough to obscure access. Deferring surgery exposes her to repeated attacks and to the complications that follow them. (Source: RANZCOG: Non obstetric surgery in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Non obstetric surgery in pregnancy

options.text: Commence oral ursodeoxycholic acid with the aim of dissolving the gallstones and preventing further episodes of her biliary pain
options.rationale: Dissolution therapy works only for small radiolucent cholesterol stones in a functioning gallbladder, takes many months and is followed by recurrence in most patients once stopped. It has no role in a woman with recurrent symptomatic multiple stones who needs definitive treatment. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Gallstone disease)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Gallstone disease

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography to define the biliary anatomy before any decision about her definitive management
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography is safe in the second trimester but is used when common bile duct stones are suspected, and normal liver tests with a 4 mm duct make that very unlikely. Ordering it here delays a decision that the ultrasound and the history have already made clear. (Source: RANZCOG: Non obstetric surgery in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Non obstetric surgery in pregnancy

explanation.summary: Gallstone disease is common in pregnancy because oestrogen increases biliary cholesterol saturation while progesterone reduces gallbladder motility, and symptomatic stones affect around one in a thousand pregnancies. Biliary colic is distinguished from cholecystitis by its complete resolution between episodes, a negative Murphy sign and normal inflammatory markers, and from choledocholithiasis by normal liver enzymes and a non dilated common bile duct. Historical practice was to defer surgery until after delivery, but this is now known to lead to recurrent admissions, and rates of preterm birth and foetal loss are higher in women managed conservatively than in those who undergo laparoscopic cholecystectomy. The second trimester is preferred because the teratogenic window has passed, the risk of miscarriage is lower than in the first trimester, and the uterus has not yet grown enough to compromise laparoscopic access or increase the risk of preterm labour. Standard laparoscopic precautions in pregnancy include left lateral tilt, open or optical entry, and lower insufflation pressures.
key_points: Complete resolution between attacks with a negative Murphy sign and normal markers indicates biliary colic.
Normal liver enzymes with a non dilated common bile duct effectively exclude duct stones.
Conservative management in pregnancy leads to recurrent attacks in over half of women.
Laparoscopic cholecystectomy in the second trimester is the preferred definitive treatment.
Left lateral tilt and lower insufflation pressures are standard modifications in pregnancy.
explanation.pearls: Gallstone pancreatitis in pregnancy carries a foetal loss rate of around 10 to 20 per cent if the gallbladder is left in place, which is why definitive cholecystectomy should follow an episode of pancreatitis during the same admission or the same trimester rather than being deferred to after birth.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Non obstetric surgery in pregnancy
Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Gallstone disease

subtopic_detail: Absent periods at sixteen with normal breasts, very sparse pubic hair and no uterus seen on pelvic ultrasound
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 16 year old girl referred because she has never had a period. Her mother reports that her breasts developed normally from about the age of eleven.

She is well, plays netball at a competitive level, has never been underweight and reports no headaches or visual symptoms. She has never been sexually active and has had no cyclical abdominal pain.

data_table.Examination: Height 175 cm, weight 64 kg, Tanner stage 5 breast development, Tanner stage 1 to 2 pubic and axillary hair, no clitoromegaly, no acne or facial hair, external genitalia otherwise normal in appearance, no palpable abdominal or inguinal masses, no goitre
data_table.Investigations: Pelvic ultrasound reporting no uterus identified with no structures in either adnexa clearly identified as ovaries, follicle stimulating hormone 6.2 IU/L (2 to 10 follicular), prolactin within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Request magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis to define the Mullerian anatomy and search for any obstructed uterine remnant
options.rationale: Imaging will follow, but it cannot distinguish the two conditions that produce an absent uterus with normal breasts, since both Mullerian agenesis and androgen insensitivity look similar on a scan. The karyotype is what separates them and it must come first. (Source: RANZCOG: Primary amenorrhoea)

options.text: Administer a progestogen challenge and interpret whether a withdrawal bleed occurs before ordering any further hormonal investigations
options.rationale: A progestogen challenge tests whether an oestrogenised endometrium is present, and this patient has no uterus at all, so the result is uninterpretable. It is a useful step in secondary amenorrhoea where the uterus is known to be present. (Source: RANZCOG: Primary amenorrhoea)

options.text: Measure a serum testosterone level and request a karyotype, and arrange review in a service with adolescent gynaecology experience
options.rationale: Full breast development with markedly sparse sexual hair and an absent uterus points to complete androgen insensitivity syndrome, in which a 46,XY individual cannot respond to androgens so the uterus regresses under anti-Mullerian hormone while oestrogen from aromatised testosterone produces normal breasts. Testosterone in the male range with a 46,XY karyotype confirms the diagnosis. (Source: RANZCOG: Primary amenorrhoea)

options.text: Start a combined oral contraceptive pill to induce regular withdrawal bleeding and review her symptoms in the clinic in three months
options.rationale: Prescribing hormones before a diagnosis is made abandons the diagnostic workup in a young woman who needs to understand her own condition and its implications for fertility and gonadal cancer risk. Oestrogen replacement has a role later, once the diagnosis and the gonadal management plan are settled. (Source: RANZCOG: Primary amenorrhoea)

options.text: Reassure her that constitutional delay is likely given her athletic training and review her again in six months if periods have not started
options.rationale: Constitutional delay and athletic amenorrhoea both involve delayed or arrested breast development from low oestrogen, whereas this young woman has completed breast development, and neither explains an absent uterus. Reassurance here would leave gonads at risk of malignancy undiagnosed. (Source: RANZCOG: Primary amenorrhoea)

explanation.summary: Primary amenorrhoea with normal breast development and an absent uterus narrows immediately to two conditions, Mullerian agenesis and complete androgen insensitivity syndrome, and the fastest way to separate them is a karyotype with a serum testosterone. In Mullerian agenesis the karyotype is 46,XX, testosterone is in the female range and pubic and axillary hair are normal because the androgen receptor works. In complete androgen insensitivity the karyotype is 46,XY, testosterone is in the male range, and sexual hair is sparse or absent precisely because the receptor does not function, while breasts develop normally from peripheral aromatisation of that testosterone. The uterus is absent because functioning testicular tissue produced anti-Mullerian hormone in utero. Management is multidisciplinary and includes careful disclosure, psychological support, oestrogen replacement after gonadectomy, vaginal dilator therapy where needed, and a decision about the timing of gonadectomy given the malignancy risk in retained intra-abdominal gonads.
key_points: Normal breasts with an absent uterus narrows to Mullerian agenesis or androgen insensitivity.
Sparse pubic and axillary hair points to androgen insensitivity rather than Mullerian agenesis.
Karyotype with serum testosterone is the discriminating investigation.
Breast development in androgen insensitivity comes from aromatisation of testosterone to oestrogen.
Care is multidisciplinary and includes psychological support and a plan for the gonads.
explanation.pearls: Gonadectomy in complete androgen insensitivity is now usually deferred until after puberty has completed spontaneously, because the malignancy risk before adulthood is under 2 per cent and allowing the endogenous gonads to drive puberty gives better bone density than early removal followed by replacement.

sources.label: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group: Differences of sex development
